title: When Your Mind Moves Faster Than Your Day
author: Matt Hutson
summary: Matt Hutson, a teacher with ADHD, offers a personal system for staying organized when ideas arrive faster than there is time to act on them. He develops three connected ideas: give your thoughts a place outside your head, let organization decide what gets your attention, and build plans that make room for changing energy. Drawing on research on cognitive offloading, reminders and task switching, he argues that writing things down frees attention and clarifies what a thought contains. He separates ideas from commitments, and proposes a planning page with four headings: Today, Next action, Ideas for later, and Restart here. He cautions against over-explaining slumps and against calling ADHD a superpower, and ends with a five-day experiment for building a modest daily habit.
points: Hutson argues that writing thoughts down gives them somewhere to live, so you do not have to keep checking yourself.
He distinguishes an idea from a commitment, so an interesting thought can be saved without becoming today's obligation.
A planning page with Today, Next action, Ideas for later and Restart here helps with choosing, starting and resuming work.
Research on task switching suggests changing direction has a cost, so batching and restart notes can make work easier.
He advises tracking energy across the day, leaving room for evenings, and seeking additional support when exhaustion persists.
quotes: But you can probably see the challenge taking shape: being excited about several things doesn’t give me several afternoons.
A notebook gives ideas a place to land, while a list gives your responsibilities somewhere you can return to.
A written reminder gives you somewhere to check instead of repeatedly checking yourself.
Having an idea does not mean you have agreed to make it your next project. You can keep it, develop it a little, or return to it when the timing makes more sense.
An idea can stay available without becoming today’s commitment. Keeping it and choosing when to act on it are separate decisions.
If you want to try this, give your planning page four simple spaces: Today, Next action, Ideas for later, and Restart here.
Experiments show that switching tasks takes time, with more complex rules leading to greater switching costs.
But the person making the plan and the person following through at five in the afternoon may have different ideas about what still feels reasonable.
